note: Curated primary studies checked on 2026-09-08. The collection includes recent work and earlier background studies; publication dates are preserved. Source checks do not establish independent replication.

items.title: Production of real signs but not pseudosigns affected by age of acquisition in American Sign Language
items.headline: Language-access history relates differently to real and invented sign production
items.authors: Shai Lynne Nielson and Rachel I. Mayberry
items.summary: Among deaf adult ASL signers, acquisition age related to handshape and movement error patterns for real signs, but not invented sign forms. This concerns task-specific production and language-access histories, not general ability.

evidence.question: Does acquisition history affect production of meaningful signs differently from invented forms?
evidence.method: Lexical decisions and repetitions in 63 deaf adults with ASL acquisition ages from birth to 14.
evidence.limitations: Observational language histories and selected repetition tasks.

explainer.finding: Acquisition age related to different component-error patterns for real signs, while invented forms showed no corresponding pattern.
explainer.method: Participants identified and repeated ASL signs and sign-like forms; researchers analyzed handshape, movement, and location errors.
explainer.meaning: Repeating a movement and integrating its form with learned meaning can place different demands on language processing.
explainer.limits: The result does not mean late learners cannot sign accurately. Early language access, later experience, and the chosen task matter; it is not an experiment randomly assigning acquisition age.

editorialReview.reason: Primary methods, results, and limitations reviewed for this language-learning collection.

items.title: Natural language processing models reveal neural dynamics of human conversation
items.headline: Natural conversation reveals signals associated with speaking, listening, and switching turns
items.summary: Intracranial recordings linked context-sensitive neural patterns to natural conversation and turn transitions. Clinical sampling and task differences prevent a complete causal explanation of conversational processing.

evidence.question: How does neural activity vary during natural dialogue?
evidence.method: Fourteen epilepsy patients conversed during recordings; model comparisons and controlled tasks probed language-related signals.
evidence.limitations: Clinically determined electrode placement; text models omit acoustic information.

explainer.finding: Speaking, listening, and their transitions showed partly overlapping, context-sensitive neural patterns.
explainer.method: Researchers related intracranial recordings to language-model representations and compared natural dialogue with controlled listening and repetition.
explainer.meaning: Answering someone involves coordinating comprehension with a planned response. Studying actual dialogue can reveal patterns missed when people only repeat prepared sentences.
explainer.limits: The clinical sample and differing task demands leave alternative explanations. Predicting neural activity with a text model does not establish that conversation is implemented by the same mechanism.

editorialReview.reason: Primary methods, results, and limitations reviewed for this language-learning collection.

items.title: Linguistic structure from a bottleneck on sequential information processing
items.headline: A constrained communication model develops word-like and phrase-like structure
items.summary: Simulated codes developed systematic local structure under an information constraint; corpus comparisons supported related patterns. The proposal assumes simplified form–meaning mappings and does not explain every ordering asymmetry.

evidence.question: Can a general information constraint explain aspects of linguistic structure?
evidence.method: Communication-code simulations and cross-language corpus comparisons with baselines.
evidence.limitations: One-to-one mappings, isolated utterances, and a time-symmetric measure.

explainer.finding: Reducing a measure of dependence between past and future produced structured codes in simulations.
explainer.method: The authors optimized artificial codes and compared statistical patterns in real-language corpora with alternatives.
explainer.meaning: Keeping related information close could help explain why language groups pieces into words and phrases. The model makes that proposal testable rather than leaving it as an intuition.
explainer.limits: This is a computational account, not a demonstration of how children learn. Ambiguity, connected discourse, and some directional word-order patterns remain outside its explanation.

editorialReview.reason: Primary methods, results, and limitations reviewed for this language-learning collection.

items.title: It’s All About In-Context Learning! Teaching Extremely Low-Resource Languages to LLMs
items.headline: Language and script coverage change which model-adaptation methods help
items.authors: Yue Li, Zhixue Zhao, and Carolina Scarton
items.summary: Across 20 underrepresented languages and three multilingual models, adaptation results varied with language and script coverage. Contextual alignment helped in especially underrepresented settings, but the tested models and datasets constrain the conclusion.

evidence.question: How can models adapt to languages poorly represented in training?
evidence.method: Comparisons of contextual prompting, language alignment, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning.
evidence.limitations: Selected models and sizes, limited parallel data, and task-specific evaluation.

explainer.finding: No adaptation method was best across every tested language and script situation.
explainer.method: Researchers compared methods across 20 languages using three multilingual models, including alignment information supplied in context.
explainer.meaning: A language poorly represented in training may need a different approach from one with more digital data. Choosing a method requires checking its actual language coverage.
explainer.limits: The findings concern the tested configurations and tasks. They do not show general fluency, reliable conversation, or that prompting always beats additional training.

editorialReview.reason: Primary methods, results, and limitations reviewed for this language-learning collection.

items.title: Mapping the neuronal building blocks of human language with language models
items.headline: Individual neurons track grammatical features during speech
items.summary: Recordings during speech linked neuronal activity to grammatical relationships and sentence context. The study involved eight English-speaking epilepsy patients; it does not establish a universal neural grammar.

evidence.question: Which linguistic features appear in neuronal activity during speech?
evidence.method: Recordings of 579 putative neurons, aligned with speech and computational linguistic annotations.
evidence.limitations: Small clinical sample, restricted recording sites, and model-dependent annotations.

explainer.finding: Some recorded neurons responded selectively to grammatical features; context helped predict population activity.
explainer.method: Researchers recorded eight epilepsy patients speaking and compared neural signals with annotated word and sentence properties.
explainer.meaning: The same noun can play different roles in different sentences. Studying those roles separately from its sound helps investigate how language is organized in the brain.
explainer.limits: These are associations in sampled brain regions during English speech. They do not show that a grammar category has one dedicated neuron everywhere, or that language models and brains work identically.

editorialReview.reason: Primary methods, results, and limitations reviewed for this language-learning collection.

items.title: Semantic similarity across languages reflects neurocognitive dimensions shaped by climate
items.headline: Word-meaning patterns vary across languages and correlate with environment
items.summary: Text representations and human ratings showed shared semantic dimensions and variation associated with climate. Corpus composition, translation mappings, and sampling limit causal and population-wide interpretations.

evidence.question: How do semantic similarities vary across languages?
evidence.method: Word embeddings from 53 languages, ratings from eight languages, and exploratory brain-data analysis.
evidence.limitations: Observational comparisons; imperfect translation equivalence and limited neural samples.

explainer.finding: The analyzed languages shared dimensions of meaning, while variation along them correlated with environmental measures.
explainer.method: Researchers compared computational word representations, speakers’ ratings, and exploratory brain data.
explainer.meaning: Dictionary equivalents need not carry identical associations. Comparing several measures helps investigate what is shared and what a translation may leave behind.
explainer.limits: The associations do not establish that climate causes an individual’s thinking. Text coverage and translation choices matter, and the small neural samples need replication.

editorialReview.reason: Primary methods, results, and limitations reviewed for this language-learning collection.

items.title: Sonority-driven stress: Codas in Brazilian Portuguese
items.headline: A word’s final sound can influence where speakers put the emphasis
items.authors: Guilherme D. Garcia and Kevin Ryan
items.venue: Glossa: a journal of general linguistics
items.summary: Brazilian Portuguese listeners favored final stress more for invented words ending in sonorants than /s/. The result concerns preferences in a small, specific sample.

evidence.question: Does consonant type affect stress placement?
evidence.method: 28 native speakers living in Canada completed pronunciation-choice tasks; lexical comparisons and Bayesian models tested the pattern.
evidence.limitations: Mostly highly educated, multilingual speakers; limited regional coverage.

explainer.finding: Sonorants, such as nasal sounds, attracted final stress more than /s/, even after checks for plural interpretations.
explainer.method: Listeners chose between pronunciations of invented words. A separate written task tested non-final positions, not the main final-syllable effect.
explainer.meaning: Invented words test patterns beyond memorized vocabulary: which syllable feels emphasized can depend on the ending’s sound.
explainer.limits: Only /s/ represented obstruents, sounds with substantial airflow obstruction. The study does not establish a universal stress rule or settle how sonority enters the grammar.

editorialReview.reason: Published author-hosted copy reviewed: methods, results, morphology checks, and theoretical limits.

items.title: The role of cognitive and linguistic abilities on subject personal pronoun expression in Spanish-speaking children
items.headline: When children say the Spanish equivalent of ‘he’ or ‘she’
items.authors: Pedro Antonio Ortiz Ramírez and colleagues
items.summary: Grammar scores helped explain pronoun use in Mexico City children; most variation remained unexplained.

evidence.question: Which abilities relate to pronoun use?
evidence.method: Interviews and language, attention, inhibition, and memory tests.
evidence.limitations: Observational, with one dialect and age range.

explainer.finding: Grammar measures retained an association with third-person pronoun use when overlapping cognitive measures were considered.
explainer.method: Researchers coded 9,750 utterances from 82 monolingual Mexican Spanish-speaking children aged four to eight and compared statistical models.
explainer.meaning: Spanish can leave the subject unstated. Choosing ‘ella’ (‘she’), for example, helps track who a story is about.
explainer.limits: Association does not establish causation or make memory irrelevant. The grammar model explained just 7.4% of variation in overall third-person pronoun use.

editorialReview.reason: Read sampling, coding, model comparisons, discussion, and scope limits. Teaches how correlated predictors can overlap.

items.title: Young Children Use the Discourse Marker “But” to Provide Clarifications in Everyday Conversations
items.headline: When a child says “but,” they may be helping you understand
items.authors: Luis De la Viña, Julia Chunxiao Hu, Paul L. Harris and Samuel Ronfard
items.summary: Seven children’s North American English conversations show increasing use of “but” to clarify earlier remarks, especially from age two to three. This small observational study cannot establish what caused the change.

evidence.question: How do children use “but” to clarify their own messages?
evidence.method: Coded 1,446 uses in longitudinal CHILDES transcripts; analyzed age patterns while accounting for individual children.
evidence.limitations: Families were predominantly highly educated; transcripts omit gesture, intonation and some shared context.

explainer.finding: Clarifications often followed adult confusion and supplied information unavailable to the listener.
explainer.method: Coders distinguished elaborations from other uses, then classified prompting and information access.
explainer.meaning: A child describing a snowman can add that it had little snow. Such a qualification helps the listener revise their picture.
explainer.limits: The study examined one English marker. It did not directly measure theory of mind or prove that conversational practice caused development.

editorialReview.reason: Read primary corpus methods, coding, results and limitations; useful illustration of conversational repair.

items.title: Implicating without intentions
items.headline: Why 'some' can suggest 'not all' without saying it
items.venue: Glossa: a journal of general linguistics
items.summary: When someone says 'some,' we often hear 'some, but not all.' This paper proposes explaining that extra meaning through what speakers commit to and are willing to disclose. Silence about a stronger claim need not signal ignorance: social rules may prevent disclosure. The analysis works through English-language examples and formal reasoning; it does not experimentally establish how listeners process them or how widely the account applies across languages.

evidence.question: Can conversational inferences be explained through commitments and disclosure expectations?
evidence.method: Formal pragmatic analysis comparing belief-based and commitment-based accounts through worked examples, including guarded speech and game-show clues. No new participant sample or behavioral experiment.
evidence.limitations: Primarily an analysis of assertions illustrated in English. Broader speech-act coverage and cross-cultural applicability remain proposals for further work.

explainer.finding: The proposed account separates having a private stance from being willing to share it. That distinction can explain why an incomplete answer sometimes suggests uncertainty and sometimes deliberate withholding.
explainer.method: The author derives inferences using formal rules for commitments, disclosure and consistency, then compares the predictions with conversational examples.
explainer.meaning: A game-show host can say the prize is in box A or box B while knowing which one. The game's rules explain why the host withholds the stronger answer; the clue need not mean the host is unsure.
explainer.limits: This is an explanatory model, not proof that intentions are irrelevant. It provides no new experiment or multilingual sample testing whether people actually use this reasoning.

editorialReview.reason: Read the primary article's competing analyses, revised formal account, worked examples and discussion. Teaches the difference between literal meaning, conversational inference and willingness to disclose. This is a theoretical proposal, with no new participant study.

items.title: Imperfectum as a window into the interaction between viewpoint aspect and telicity: A view from Torlak
items.venue: Glossa: a journal of general linguistics
items.headline: How completed events can become a recurring habit in grammar
items.summary: A completed action and an ongoing habit are different things. Torlak, a South Slavic variety, can combine perfective verb stems with a past imperfect form when describing habits. A study documents this pattern in speech and proposes that the grammar groups individual bounded events into a recurring series. The observed pattern challenges a simple ban on this combination; the proposed grammatical structure remains a theoretical explanation, not an experimentally established universal.

evidence.question: How can Torlak combine perfective stems with an imperfective viewpoint without losing their meaning as bounded events?
evidence.method: Analyzed 195 lexical-verb imperfectum tokens from a dataset based on a spoken Timok Torlak corpus, alongside a description of Jablanica Torlak and the author’s native-speaker judgments. Uncertain judgments were checked with two additional speakers. Compared forms, clause types and interpretations, then developed a formal semantic analysis.
evidence.limitations: This is corpus-supported grammatical analysis, not a representative speaker survey or controlled learning experiment. Repeated common verbs affect token proportions. The data concern particular Torlak varieties; broader cross-language extensions require further investigation.

explainer.finding: Perfective stems occurred in 26 of 195 tokens, including 19 in main clauses. The author argues that these forms are productive in habitual descriptions rather than merely rare exceptions.
explainer.method: The analysis separates an event’s internal endpoint from the viewpoint taken on it. A proposed grammatical layer groups bounded events into a series that can support an imperfective description of a habit.
explainer.meaning: As an English analogy, compare finishing one cake with regularly finishing a cake every Sunday. Each cake-making event has an endpoint, but the recurring habit need not have one. The study asks how Torlak expresses that distinction inside its verb forms.
explainer.limits: The corpus counts support the existence and distribution of the forms. They do not uniquely prove the proposed hidden grammatical layers. The account’s predictions for other Slavic and Romance languages remain hypotheses.

editorialReview.reason: Read corpus counts and annotation description, speaker-judgment provenance, core aspectual analysis and cross-language limitations. Teaches the distinction between bounded events and viewpoint; labels the formal structure as a proposal.

items.title: Islands satiate without change in backgroundedness
items.headline: Awkward questions can grow more acceptable without changing their background meaning
items.venue: Glossa: a journal of general linguistics
items.summary: Why does a question sound wrong, and can familiarity change that judgment? In two experiments with native English speakers, repeated exposure reduced the extra acceptability penalty for questions that reach into certain tightly grouped sentence structures, called syntactic islands. A separate task found no corresponding change in whether the information inside those structures was treated as background. That challenges an explanation based entirely on background information, but does not settle the grammatical mechanism: only two specific English constructions were tested, and the penalty did not disappear.

evidence.question: Does repeated exposure reduce an island penalty by changing how readers interpret the background status of the information inside it?
evidence.method: Two Prolific experiments recruited 300 native English speakers each; analyses retained 294 and 285. Four exposure blocks crossed island versus non-island structure with shorter versus longer dependencies. Mixed-effects models tested changes in the interaction between those factors. Before and after exposure, interpretation questions compared affirmative and negated sentences; Bayesian analyses assessed evidence for no change in that contrast.
evidence.limitations: Acceptability ratings and the negation task are operational measures, not direct observations of grammar. Results cover complex noun phrases headed by claim and definite subjects containing by-phrases. Null interpretation results cannot exclude every small change, and familiarity, learning and greater tolerance remain possible explanations.

explainer.finding: Some questions became less awkward with exposure, even though the measured background status of their information stayed stable. Both construction types retained an island penalty.
explainer.method: Readers rated questions on a continuous scale. Comparing four sentence types helped isolate the extra penalty for combining a long dependency with an island structure. Separate interpretation questions before and after exposure tested whether background meaning changed too.
explainer.meaning: Compare ‘What did Mia say that Leo bought?’ with ‘What did Mia discuss the claim that Leo bought?’ The latter asks the reader to connect ‘what’ to a position inside ‘the claim.’ Such contrasts let researchers test why a construction feels awkward, rather than assume that improved ratings mean its interpretation changed.
explainer.limits: The study concerns particular English sentences in an online task. It neither proves that repetition rewrites grammar nor rules out a role for discourse. The authors report evidence supporting the null interpretation result, while acknowledging that a smaller undetected change remains possible.

editorialReview.reason: Read primary full text, both experiments' methods and results, discussion and limitations. The factorial rating design separates the island penalty from additive structure and dependency-length effects; the negation task supplies a distinct interpretation measure. Publisher citation metadata dates the article October 20, unlike Crossref discovery October 21.
